title: QuickBasket
pitch: You and a friend left your jobs to start a 10-minute grocery delivery app in Pune. You have ₹2 crore from angel investors, a small team and a big rival that could arrive any day. In about two years you must reach 50,000 monthly users, earn as much as you spend each month, and keep people's trust.

stages.title: Find the real problem
stages.situation: Before building anything, you want to understand how people in Pune buy groceries today. You have one month.

options.label: Run an online survey of 2,000 people
options.detail: Fast and cheap. Lots of data.

later.note: Your survey said people wanted 'more choice'. In practice they wanted reliability. Users who joined for choice are leaving.

options.outcome: 2,000 replies in a week. Most people say they want more choice and lower prices.
options.lesson: What people say in surveys and what they do are often different. Surveys are good for 'how many', not 'why'.

options.label: Shadow 30 families and 10 kirana shops for 3 weeks
options.detail: Slow, but you see real behaviour.
options.outcome: You learn the real pain: people run out of 2 or 3 items in the evening and the kirana is closed or out of stock.
options.lesson: Watching real people shows the problem behind the request. That insight shapes everything you build next.

options.label: Skip research and copy what Blinkit does
options.detail: It already works in other cities.
options.outcome: You save a month. But you don't know what Pune users specifically need.
options.lesson: Copying a leader copies their answers without their reasons. You'll struggle to be better than them.

stages.title: Pick your first users
stages.situation: You can only serve one group well at first. Who do you build for?

options.label: Young professionals in Baner and Hinjewadi flats
options.detail: Dense area, busy people, order often.
options.outcome: Many orders from a small area. Riders make short trips.
options.lesson: Dense, frequent users make a delivery business work. Start where orders are close together.

options.label: Families across all of Pune
options.outcome: Bigger orders, but riders travel far and costs climb.
options.lesson: A big market that is spread out is expensive to serve. Density beats size early on.

options.label: College students in hostels
options.outcome: Lots of sign ups, small orders, many coupon hunters.
options.lesson: Fast adopters aren't always good customers. Check basket size and repeat rate, not just sign ups.

later.note: Exams and summer break: students went home and many never came back.

stages.title: Decide what to build first
stages.situation: Time to build the first version. What goes in it?

options.label: One dark store, 600 top items, simple app
options.outcome: Few items, but almost everything is in stock and arrives in 12 minutes.
options.lesson: An MVP should do the core job very well. Reliability on a few items beats choice that often fails.

options.label: Three dark stores, 5,000 items, full app
options.detail: Look like a big player from day one.
options.outcome: Impressive launch, but stock runs out often and costs are high.
options.lesson: Building too much before learning burns cash and spreads the team thin.

options.label: No stores: partner with 20 kirana shops
options.outcome: Cheap to run, but delivery takes 30 to 40 minutes and items are often missing.
options.lesson: Not owning the core of your promise (speed and stock) makes it hard to keep it.

stages.title: Set your prices
stages.situation: How will you price products and delivery?

options.label: MRP prices with a ₹25 fee under ₹199
options.outcome: Some people grumble about the fee, but each order makes a little money.
options.lesson: A small, clear fee teaches users that speed has a price, and protects your margin.

options.label: 20% off everything to win users
options.detail: Grow fast now, fix money later.

later.note: You cut the 20% discount to stop the losses. Many deal hunters left with it.

options.outcome: Orders pour in. Every order loses money.
options.lesson: Discounts buy users who love discounts. When the discount goes, so do they.

options.label: Free delivery with a ₹99 monthly pass
options.outcome: Pass holders order twice as often as others.
options.lesson: Memberships turn occasional users into regulars, because people want to get value from what they paid.

stages.title: Launch to the public
stages.situation: You're ready to launch. How do you find your first big wave of users?

options.label: Society WhatsApp groups and RWA tie-ups
options.outcome: Word spreads society by society. Neighbours recommend you.
options.lesson: Trusted local channels bring users who stay, and they are cheap.

options.label: ₹30 lakh on Instagram ads and influencers

later.note: Many users who came from ads tried you once and never came back.

options.outcome: Downloads spike. Many people order once out of curiosity.
options.lesson: Paid reach brings tourists. Check how many come back before you spend more.

options.label: Referral offer: ₹100 for both friends
options.outcome: Happy users invite friends. Some people farm the reward with fake accounts.
options.lesson: Referrals work when users already love you. Pay the reward after the friend's first real order to stop fraud.

stages.title: Fix the second order
stages.situation: 45% of new users never place a second order. What do you fix?

options.label: Fix out-of-stock items and wrong substitutions
options.outcome: Complaints fall. More people come back within a week.
options.lesson: The first order is a promise. If it fails, no notification will bring the user back.

options.label: Send 3 push notifications a day
options.outcome: Some come back. Many mute or uninstall the app.
options.lesson: Spam is not retention. Notifications work only when they're timely and useful.

options.label: ₹75 off the second order
options.outcome: Second orders rise, but many stop after the coupon.
options.lesson: Coupons can start a habit, but they can't fix a bad experience.

stages.title: Choose your north star
stages.situation: The team is growing and pulling in different directions. Which single number will everyone chase?

options.label: Weekly orders delivered on time and complete
options.outcome: Ops, product and growth teams finally pull in the same direction.
options.lesson: A good north star counts the moment users get value. It lines up every team.

options.label: App downloads
options.outcome: Marketing celebrates. Ops is ignored. Quality slips.
options.lesson: Vanity metrics go up while the business gets worse.

options.label: Total order value (GMV)
options.outcome: The team pushes big baskets with discounts. Value goes up, margin goes down.
options.lesson: GMV can be bought. A north star should be hard to fake.

stages.title: Grow the team
stages.situation: Founders are exhausted. You can afford one hiring plan.

options.label: Hire 2 experienced ops leaders
options.detail: Expensive, but they've done this before.
options.outcome: Stores run smoother. Founders can think about strategy again.
options.lesson: In an operations business, great ops leaders are worth their salary.

options.label: Hire 10 junior developers
options.outcome: Lots of features ship. Stores are still chaotic.
options.lesson: More features don't fix an operations problem. Hire for your real bottleneck.

later.note: Features shipped fast without senior review. Bugs in checkout are pushing users away.

options.label: Stay lean, founders do everything
options.outcome: You save money. Founders sleep 4 hours a night and start making mistakes.
options.lesson: Burnout is a real cost, even if it doesn't show in the bank balance.

later.note: Exhausted founders made costly mistakes: a wrong stock order and a missed payroll.

stages.title: Raise money
stages.situation: Investors are interested. Which deal do you take?

options.label: ₹10 crore, promise 5 new cities in a year

later.note: To keep your promise, you opened stores in new cities before Pune was profitable. Costs exploded.

options.outcome: The bank account looks amazing. The board expects fast expansion.
options.lesson: Money comes with expectations. Big promises can force you to grow before you're ready.

options.label: ₹3 crore from operator angels
options.outcome: Your new investors ran delivery businesses before. Their advice saves you mistakes.
options.lesson: The right investors bring more than money. Raise what you need to hit the next milestone.

options.label: Don't raise. Aim for profit.
options.outcome: No dilution, but you can't move fast if a rival arrives.
options.lesson: Bootstrapping keeps control but limits speed. In a race, cash is fuel.

stages.title: Build a growth engine
stages.situation: Pune is working. Where do you put the next big effort?

options.label: Open 4 more dark stores in dense areas
options.outcome: More homes can order. Each store takes 3 months to fill up.
options.lesson: Supply unlocks demand in delivery. But each store has to earn back its cost.

options.label: TV ads during the IPL

later.note: IPL viewers outside your delivery areas installed the app, found nothing, and left angry.

options.outcome: Huge awareness. Many viewers live where you don't deliver.
options.lesson: Don't advertise beyond where you can deliver. Awareness without availability creates angry users.

options.label: Add a café: hot coffee and snacks in 10 minutes
options.detail: A daily habit, not just a weekly one.
options.outcome: People who order coffee every morning also buy groceries more often.
options.lesson: A daily-use feature builds habit and lifts everything else.

stages.title: Earn more per order
stages.situation: You still lose a little on many orders. How do you earn more?

options.label: Sell ad spots to FMCG brands
options.outcome: Brands pay well. Users barely notice a few sponsored items.
options.lesson: Ads on a shopping app can be almost pure profit, if they stay relevant.

options.label: Raise the delivery fee to ₹39
options.outcome: Money per order rises. Social media fills with angry posts.
options.lesson: Raising prices works only if users value you enough. Watch cancellations closely.

options.label: Launch your own brand of staples
options.detail: Atta, rice and dal with better margins.

later.note: Your own-brand staples took off. Margins on them are double.

options.outcome: Slow start. Users need time to trust a new brand.
options.lesson: Private labels take time but build lasting margin.

stages.title: A giant arrives
stages.situation: A national quick commerce giant launches in Pune with 50% off for three months.

options.label: Match their discounts

later.note: The price war ended. Your discounts stopped, the cash is gone, and deal hunters left for whoever is cheapest next.

options.outcome: You keep users but burn cash fast.
options.lesson: A price war against a richer rival is a war of bank balances. You'll usually lose.

options.label: Ignore price. Double down on reliability and your pass.
options.detail: Compete on what you do best.

later.note: The giant's discounts ended. Users who wanted reliability came back to you.

options.outcome: You lose some deal hunters for a while.
options.lesson: Compete where you're strong. Loyal users come back when the free money stops.

options.label: Pivot to supplying kirana shops (B2B)
options.outcome: Steadier money, but your consumer app shrinks.
options.lesson: Pivots can save a company, but they throw away what you built. Make sure the old plan is truly dead.

stages.title: A video goes viral
stages.situation: A customer posts a video of expired milk from your store. It has 2 million views.

options.label: Apologise publicly, refund everyone, add daily freshness checks
options.outcome: People respect the honesty. The story fades in a week.
options.lesson: Own mistakes fast and fix the system behind them. Trust can even grow after a crisis handled well.

options.label: Send a legal notice to take the video down
options.outcome: The legal notice itself goes viral. Now it's a bigger story.
options.lesson: Trying to hide a problem usually makes it bigger.

options.label: Blame the supplier in a public statement
options.outcome: Users don't care whose fault it was. They bought it from you.
options.lesson: Users hold the brand responsible, not your suppliers.

stages.title: Riders go on strike
stages.situation: Delivery riders strike over falling pay. Orders are stuck.

options.label: Raise pay per order and add accident insurance
options.outcome: Riders return. Costs per order rise a little.
options.lesson: Your supply side are people too. Fair pay is part of a healthy marketplace.

options.label: Replace them with riders from an agency
options.outcome: New riders don't know the area. Deliveries are late for weeks.
options.lesson: Cheap replacements can cost more than they save.

options.label: Batch 2 orders per trip and share the savings with riders
options.outcome: Riders earn more per trip. Some deliveries take 15 minutes instead of 10.
options.lesson: Look for solutions where both sides win, then be honest about the trade-off.

stages.title: The road to profit
stages.situation: The board wants a clear path to earning more than you spend. What's your final big move?

options.label: Close the weakest 30% of stores
options.outcome: Costs fall sharply. Some users lose 10-minute delivery.
options.lesson: Cutting what doesn't work is as important as adding what does.

options.label: Expand to Mumbai now
options.outcome: Users jump, but so do costs, in a new city you don't know yet.
options.lesson: Expanding before the core city is profitable multiplies losses.

options.label: Raise prices 5% on everything
options.outcome: Margins improve. Some users notice and complain.
options.lesson: Small price changes add up, but they spend some of your users' goodwill.

events.title: Monsoon floods
events.situation: Heavy rain floods half the city for three days. Orders triple but roads are dangerous.

options.label: Pause deliveries in flooded areas, tell users why
options.outcome: Users understand. Riders are safe.
options.lesson: Safety first. Clear communication keeps trust when you can't deliver.

options.label: Add a ₹50 rain fee and keep going
options.outcome: Revenue jumps. Two riders are hurt.
options.lesson: Short-term money at the cost of people's safety damages your brand and team.

events.title: Payments go down
events.situation: Your payment partner has an outage on a Saturday evening, your busiest time.

options.label: Switch on cash on delivery right away
options.outcome: Orders keep flowing. Some cash goes missing.
options.lesson: Have a backup for every critical part of the journey.

options.label: Wait for the partner to fix it
options.outcome: Three hours of failed orders. Users try another app.
options.lesson: Users don't care whose system failed. They only see your app failing.

events.title: A rival poaches your ops head
events.situation: A big rival offers your head of operations double the salary.

options.label: Counter-offer with more equity
options.outcome: They stay. Others notice you fight for your people.
options.lesson: Keeping a key person is usually cheaper than replacing them.

options.label: Let them go and promote from within
options.outcome: The new lead is eager but learning on the job.
options.lesson: Promoting from within builds loyalty, but plan for a dip while they learn.

events.title: Diwali rush
events.situation: Diwali week is coming. Orders could double.

options.label: Stock up early and add temporary staff
options.outcome: A record week, with few stock-outs.
options.lesson: Plan for peaks. Your best week can win users for the whole year.

options.label: Run as normal
options.outcome: Shelves empty by Tuesday. Users go elsewhere.
options.lesson: Being unprepared at peak moments sends users to rivals.
